opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think the main problem was that in 2021 we didn't really understand what we were scaling, or why. Many teams, including the one I was close to at the time, saw GPT-3 and concluded the lesson was "make the model bigger." So people trained very large models, some with hundreds of billions or even trillions of parameters through mixture-of-experts. But the results were underwhelming. The models were big on paper but not much smarter in practice.

I'd point to a few reasons.

First, data. People focused on parameter count and neglected data quality and quantity. Later work on compute-optimal scaling made it clear that many of those models were badly undertrained relative to their size. You had a huge model that had seen too few tokens, and the tokens it did see were often noisy web data that wasn't carefully cleaned or deduplicated. Data engineering wasn't treated as core research then. Now we know it's probably the most important part.

Second, the goal itself. At that time, the computer vision community, which is where I came from, still had a "pretrain, then fine-tune on downstream tasks" mindset. We evaluated large models on benchmarks one task at a time. We didn't fully appreciate that the real value of a language model is that it compresses a huge amount of knowledge and reasoning into one general system you can talk to. Without instruction tuning and alignment, which only became clear with ChatGPT at the end of 2022, even a decent base model doesn't *feel* impressive. So part of the disappointment was that we didn't know how to unlock what was there.

Third, infrastructure and engineering maturity. Training at that scale stably is very hard. Loss spikes, numerical issues, inefficient parallelism. A lot of compute was wasted, and many teams simply couldn't run enough experiments to learn the right recipes. The scaling laws are only useful if you can actually follow them carefully at small scale and extrapolate. Most groups didn't have that discipline yet.

And finally, honestly, conviction. In 2021 many people, myself included to some degree, didn't fully believe that language was the right path to general intelligence. In vision we kept hoping that something like the GPT moment would come from images, from self-supervised learning on pixels. It didn't happen that way. Language turned out to be special because it's already a highly compressed, human-curated representation of knowledge and reasoning. Once you accept that, you invest differently: in data, in tokens, in alignment, not just in parameters.

So it wasn't that large models were the wrong idea. It was that we had the right direction with the wrong recipe and not enough understanding of why it worked.

r001.rationale: The response says teams neglected data quality and used noisy web data that was not carefully cleaned or deduplicated.

r002.rationale: It connects teams’ post-GPT-3 efforts to build very large models with models that were badly undertrained relative to their size because they had seen too few tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that in 2021 most of us, myself included, misunderstood what "large model" actually meant.

Back then, when people in China talked about big models, the thing everyone focused on was the parameter count. Wudao, Pangu, all those efforts were racing to a trillion parameters, and the implicit assumption was that the number itself was the breakthrough. But scale is not one knob. It's at least three: parameters, data, and compute. And if you only turn one of them, you get a model that is big but badly undertrained. A lot of the 2021 models had enormous parameter counts but were fed a fraction of the tokens they needed. DeepMind's Chinchilla paper in 2022 made this explicit, but in hindsight you could already see it in the results.

The second problem was data quality. People treated data as something you crawl and dump in. There wasn't much appreciation for cleaning, deduplication, mixing ratios, or how much the composition of the corpus shapes the model's behavior. Those are unglamorous engineering problems, and they didn't get the attention or the headcount they deserved.

Third, and I think this is the deeper issue, there was no clear sense of what the model was for. It was large model as a demonstration, a benchmark number, a press release. Nobody had really thought through the gap between a pretrained base model and something a person would actually want to use. That's what alignment and instruction tuning turned out to fill, and it's why ChatGPT at the end of 2022 felt like such a discontinuity even though the underlying model wasn't that different from what existed in 2021.

And finally, the organizational side. Training a model like this is fundamentally a systems and infrastructure problem, not just an algorithm problem. Most research groups in 2021 were structured for writing papers, not for running a single training job across thousands of GPUs for months without the loss spiking and nobody knowing why. The teams that eventually did well were the ones that treated it as engineering first.

So I wouldn't say 2021 was a failure. It was more like tuition. We paid to learn that bigger was necessary but very far from sufficient.

r001.rationale: The response says data quality was a problem and describes insufficient cleaning, deduplication, and corpus composition.

r002.rationale: It says 2021 models were undertrained because they had too few tokens for their parameter counts, but it does not identify them as attempts to reproduce GPT-3.

astra-6.text:
My sense is that we focused too much on making models bigger and too little on what would make them useful. A larger parameter count was an easy milestone to communicate, but it didn’t necessarily translate into a clear improvement for users.

You need the other pieces to develop together: data quality, training methods, evaluation, and a concrete understanding of the tasks you want the model to perform. If you increase scale while those pieces remain weak, you can spend a lot more without getting a proportionate return.

So I’d distinguish disappointment in the models from disappointment in the expectations. The research could still be valuable, but the expectation that a very large model would immediately become a useful product was ahead of what those efforts could deliver.

r001.rationale: The response says data quality needs to develop alongside scale and that weak supporting elements can limit returns, attributing disappointment partly to weak data quality.

r002.rationale: It does not mention GPT-3 reproduction, undertraining, or training-token counts being too small relative to parameter counts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main issue was that people treated model size as the goal. Once scaling looked promising, the question became, “How many parameters can we build?” But a larger model doesn’t automatically become a more useful model. The data, the training process, and the amount of compute all have to fit together. If you increase the parameter count without getting those other pieces right, the return can be quite limited.

There was also a gap between demonstrating a capability and making it useful. A model might generate an impressive passage, but still struggle to follow a user’s instructions consistently or complete a practical task. So I wouldn’t say the work in 2021 had no value. It built experience and infrastructure. But the expectations got ahead of what simply making models bigger could deliver.

r001.rationale: It says the data must fit with model size, training, and compute, but does not attribute the disappointing results to poor training-data quality.

r002.rationale: It does not mention GPT-3 reproduction attempts, training-token counts, or models being undertrained relative to their parameter counts.
